item.title: Anxiety Is Alpha-Gal Syndrome’s Overlooked Side Effect
item.description:
Anxiety

Anxiety Is Alpha-Gal Syndrome’s Overlooked Side Effect

Lone star tick bites can lead to much more than a red meat allergy.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Alpha-gal syndrome is a tick-borne disease that involves an allergy to mammalian products such as red meat.
  • Anxiety is a common side effect of alpha-gal syndrome, affecting up to 3 in 5 individuals with the condition.
  • Food allergy anxiety is under researched and can be more complicated to treat than other anxiety disorders.
  • Mental health screening in high-risk areas and piloting behavioral therapy for alpha gal are promising.
Source: Kampus Productions / Pexels

I first learned about alpha-gal syndrome in the back corner of a tavern in Southwest Virginia as my aunt carefully unwrapped cellophane from a turkey sandwich she’d just pulled from her handbag. We were at a family birthday party, seated near an inviting spread of wood-fired pizzas laid out for guests. She noticed my quizzical look at the deli turkey. “It’s because of alpha-gal,” she said, and produced a small stack of printed papers from the same handbag. “I made these to give out at restaurants and to my doctors, because so many people still don’t know about it.”

As I scanned the homemade flyer and listened to my aunt’s stories, what I learned sounded like something from a sci-fi novel. Tick bites can lead to developing a severe, even life-threatening allergic reaction to mammalian products? The disease is spreading across Southern Appalachia such that not one, but two of my aunts had developed meat allergies in the past year? My aunt was surprisingly matter-of-fact as she explained the list of products she had to avoid (beef, pork, dairy) as well as her trips to the emergency room when she’d unknowingly ingested them. As I finished my second slice of meatlovers, I couldn’t help but think that she was coping remarkably well with this life-changing new allergy.

What Is Alpha-Gal Syndrome?

Alpha-gal syndrome is a tick-borne, allergic disease. The sugar molecule called “alpha-gal” (galactose-α-1,3-galactose) is produced by many non-primate mammals and some pests, particularly lone star ticks. If this tick bites a human, it can transfer these molecules to the bloodstream, causing the immune system to react when that person is further exposed to the alpha-gal molecule in mammalian products. Not all individuals bitten by an alpha-gal-carrying tick will develop alpha-gal syndrome. Many will become asymptomatically sensitized; they will not have any allergic reactions after eating red meat, but could be at risk of developing an allergy to mammalian products in the future.

Several factors make alpha-gal syndrome confusing and difficult to diagnose compared with other food allergies. Unlike traditional allergies, alpha-gal syndrome symptoms do not appear rapidly; they typically start two to six hours after consuming the allergen. In the interim, the individual may have had multiple other meals or exposures, which may confound the connection directly to the allergen. Adults who have eaten red meat all of their lives can acquire alpha-gal syndrome, leaving them unsuspecting of mammalian products as the cause. Symptoms of allergic reactions can vary greatly in alpha-gal patients, but can also present differently in the same individual. Symptoms can include hives, GI symptoms, itchy skin, facial swelling, shortness of breath, wheezing, coughing, and anaphylaxis.

Although alpha-gal syndrome has been found across the United States, it is highly concentrated in areas with a prevalence of lone star ticks. The most cases have been reported in the Southern, Midwestern, and Mid-Atlantic regions. One study estimated 450,000 cases of alpha-gal syndrome in the US. Another study, published earlier this summer, found that nearly one in four individuals living in the most affected states (Arkansas, Kentucky, Missouri, Tennessee, and Virginia) tested positive for alpha-gal antibodies. Living in a rural area, having an outdoor lifestyle, and being male increase the risk of alpha-gal syndrome, likely because these factors are also associated with higher tick exposure. Alpha-gal syndrome has been found on other continents, with notable concentrations in Central Europe, Japan, South Korea, the East Coast of Australia, and the Eastern Cape of South Africa.

Why Anxiety Matters in Food Allergies

Allergy-related anxiety and panic symptoms are widespread but underaddressed, with one study suggesting that nearly two-thirds of individuals living with food allergies suffer from mental health concerns. In an exploratory survey of more than 2,000 patients with alpha-gal syndrome, 60 percent of participants reported experiencing anxiety related to the condition. In fact, across seven categories of symptoms assessed (gastrointestinal, integumentary, respiratory, cardiovascular, autonomic, muscular, and behavioral/emotional), anxiety was the most frequently reported symptom.

Several factors make food allergy anxiety qualitatively different from other types of anxiety such as a specific phobia or generalized anxiety:

  1. Food allergies pose a valid threat. For someone with a phobia of lightning, statistics suggest their chance of being struck is extremely low. Their irrational fears may respond well to basic cognitive testing with a psychotherapist. However, allergic reactions to food can be life-threatening, and research suggests that mental health concerns are more common for individuals who have had more than one reaction per year.
  2. Panic attacks mimic allergic reactions. Panic attacks can include symptoms such as shortness of breath, sensations of choking, chest pain, nausea, and dizziness—all symptoms that are also associated with allergic reactions and anaphylaxis. While anaphylaxis requires immediate medical intervention, panic attacks typically peak within 10 minutes and are not inherently harmful to the body. It can be difficult for someone anxious about food to distinguish whether they are having a true allergic reaction or a panic attack.
  3. For people with alpha-gal syndrome, certain psychiatric medications are off the table. Mammalian products are commonly used as inactive ingredients in medications. For example, buspirone and pregabalin are sometimes used to treat anxiety, and both contain mammalian products that may be dangerous for those with alpha-gal syndrome. Prescribers treating anxiety in alpha-gal patients must be aware of these ingredients when considering a psychotropic medication.

Promising Directions for Anxiety and Alpha-Gal

We have much to do to address the spread of alpha-gal syndrome, including the anxiety that the condition can cause. Mental health screening is needed for patients testing positive for alpha-gal syndrome, and should be a particular focus in high-risk areas, such as rural health care settings and areas with high prevalence. Patient education may quell anxiety, including education about food avoidance, proper use of epinephrine autoinjectors, and how to access emergency medical services quickly. Cognitive behavioral therapy is a first-line treatment for anxiety disorders and has lots of empirical support. Although treatments for anxiety in food allergies are understudied, particularly in adults, there is evidence to suggest that such therapy is helpful for children with food allergies and their caretakers. The theoretical underpinnings of the treatment likely transfer well to adults with alpha-gal who are suffering from anxiety, teaching them to address unhelpful thoughts and behaviors and cope more effectively with allergy-related fears.
